title: Cloned family voice used in an emergency money request
shortParaphrase: A caller uses a cloned version of a family member's voice to claim the person is in serious trouble and needs money immediately. The FTC advises independently calling the relative or another trusted person at a known number before acting.
requestedActions: send money for the claimed emergency

source.title: Scammers use AI to enhance their family emergency schemes

notes: FTC warning about voice-cloning in family-emergency scams.

title: Fake friend or family emergency demands immediate payment
shortParaphrase: A caller pretends to be a family member or close friend, or someone acting for them, and claims an urgent crisis. The caller uses secrecy and emotional pressure to demand a hard-to-recover payment before the story can be checked.
claimedIdentity: family member, close friend, or helper

source.title: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money

notes: The evergreen FTC article displays a month and year, so no precise day is stored.

title: Unexpected online task offer followed by deposit request
shortParaphrase: An unexpected WhatsApp, Telegram, text, or social message offers simple paid online tasks. Apparent earnings may be shown or a small payment may be sent, then the victim is told to deposit personal funds to continue or withdraw supposed earnings.

source.title: How to spot and avoid task scams

notes: Reference example retained from the first vertical slice.

title: Fake work-from-home tasks require cryptocurrency deposits
shortParaphrase: A fake work-from-home offer promises payment for simple optimization-style tasks and displays supposed earnings on a fraudulent interface. The target is told to make cryptocurrency payments to unlock more work or earnings.
requestedActions: send cryptocurrency to unlock work or earnings

source.organizationOrPublisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center
source.title: Scammers Defraud Individuals via Work-From-Home Scams

notes: FBI IC3 public service announcement about fake work-from-home task schemes.

title: Online love interest moves the conversation and asks for money
shortParaphrase: A new contact on a dating app or social platform builds a frequent personal relationship, asks to continue talking away from the original platform, cannot meet in person, and eventually asks for money or promotes an investment.
requestedActions: move the conversation off the platform

source.title: Looking for love? Watch out for scammers

notes: FTC warning about romance scams that progress to money or investment requests.

title: Online relationship turns into a cryptocurrency investment pitch
shortParaphrase: A stranger contacts someone on social media, develops an emotional connection, and then offers to teach them to invest in cryptocurrency. The scam promises large profits with little or no risk and directs the target to send money quickly.
claimedIdentity: online romantic interest and investment guide

source.title: What to do if your online love interest offers to teach you how to invest your money

notes: FTC warning about romance-based cryptocurrency investment fraud.

title: Government impersonator threatens consequences and demands payment
shortParaphrase: A caller or message pretends to come from a government agency and claims payment or personal information is urgently required to prevent arrest, loss of benefits, or another serious consequence.
requestedActions: send payment using a hard-to-recover method

source.title: How To Avoid a Government Impersonation Scam

notes: The evergreen FTC article does not expose a reliably verified full publication date.

title: Agency impersonator orders funds moved to a secure account
shortParaphrase: A scammer impersonates the FTC, another agency, or a familiar organization, escalates an ordinary account problem into a claim of criminal activity, and pressures the target to move savings, buy cryptocurrency or gold, or hand over cash for supposed protection.
requestedActions: transfer money to a supposedly secure account
buy cryptocurrency, gold, or withdraw cash

source.title: Did someone tell you to move or transfer your money? It could be a scam

notes: FTC warning about institution impostors directing victims to move assets.

title: Fake marketplace buyer uses payment and verification tricks
shortParaphrase: A fake buyer insists on a mobile payment method, sends a false payment notice, claims an overpayment, or asks for a verification code supposedly to confirm the seller is real. The seller may be pushed to refund money or disclose the code.
requestedActions: send money back after a claimed payment

source.title: Selling stuff online? Here’s how to avoid a scam

notes: FTC warning covering fake buyer payments, overpayments, and verification-code requests.

title: Marketplace seller asks a buyer to pay outside platform protections
shortParaphrase: A seller asks a marketplace buyer to use a wire transfer, gift card, cryptocurrency, or another payment method outside the marketplace's system, making it difficult to dispute the transaction or recover the money.
notes: The evergreen FTC article displays a month and year, so no precise day is stored.

title: Fake security pop-up warns of a device infection
shortParaphrase: A bogus pop-up or message claims a computer has a serious security problem or virus and creates pressure to contact a supposed technical-support service using the displayed number.

source.title: How To Spot, Avoid, and Report Tech Support Scams

notes: Fake-warning variant documented by the FTC; the evergreen page exposes no reliably verified full date.

title: Fake technician seeks remote access and payment
shortParaphrase: A supposed technician claims to find viruses or hacked accounts, asks for remote access to the target's computer, and then demands payment or directs the target to move money using methods that are difficult to reverse.
requestedActions: grant remote access to the computer
pay for supposed support or move money

source.title: How To Spot, Avoid, and Report Tech Support Scams

notes: Remote-access and payment variant documented by the same FTC source.

title: Compromised business email redirects a legitimate funds transfer
shortParaphrase: A criminal compromises a legitimate business or personal email account through social engineering or intrusion and uses the trusted professional workflow to direct an unauthorized transfer of funds.
requestedActions: complete a fraudulent transfer of funds

source.organizationOrPublisher: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Internet Crime Complaint Center
source.title: Business Email Compromise: The $55 Billion Scam

notes: FBI IC3 public service announcement about business email compromise and fraudulent transfers.

title: Fake recruiter or developer collaboration delivers malicious code
shortParaphrase: A threat actor approaches a technology worker using a fake or compromised recruiter or developer identity, may move the conversation across professional or messaging platforms, and invites collaboration on a repository containing malicious npm dependencies or sends software to run.
requestedActions: move the professional conversation to another platform
clone and execute a repository or install software

source.title: Security alert: social engineering campaign targets technology industry employees

notes: GitHub Security account of a campaign using professional collaboration to deliver malicious software.

title: Trusted-company phishing email uses an invoice attachment lure
shortParaphrase: An unexpected email impersonates a familiar bank, utility, or other company and claims there is an overdue invoice or account problem. It asks the recipient to open an attachment or click a link, exposing them to malware or information theft.
notes: FTC warning about unexpected invoice-themed phishing links and attachments.

title: Invoice-named PDF attachment delivers banking malware
shortParaphrase: A phishing email uses an ordinary invoice-named PDF as the lure. Opening the weaponized attachment can download Dyre banking malware, turning a routine business document into the path to infection.

source.title: Phishing Campaign Linked with “Dyre” Banking Malware

notes: CISA-hosted US-CERT alert, originally published October 27, 2014 and revised September 30, 2016.
